Keyword co-occurrence and citation-network analysis need a document's
author-supplied keywords and its own reference list, which the Search API alone
does not return. This article covers how to retrieve them, what each costs and
what your 'Scopus' entitlement needs to cover.

The API calls below are shown as you would run them with a configured key, and
they are not run here, so no output appears beneath them. No key is available
when the site and the package are built, and Elsevier's terms do not permit
redistributing retrieved records in any case. The shapes the calls return are
built in view from `example_records`, the bundled harvest of real papers that
the other articles run on. That harvest carries neither author keywords nor
reference lists, so its records and titles are relabelled into those shapes, and
the text says each time what stands in for what. A script of your own can use
`scopus_has_key()` to run the calls only when a key is configured.

```{r setup}
library(scopusflow)
```

## Author keywords from a search

The Search API's `COMPLETE` view carries an `authkeywords` field alongside the
usual title, DOI and date. The field adds no request of its own, but `COMPLETE`
serves 25 records per page, against 200 for `STANDARD`. The same number of
records therefore already takes more requests and more quota.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
recs <- scopus_fetch("DOI(10.1038/nature14539)", view = "COMPLETE")
recs$authkeywords
```

The column holds one string per record, with the keywords joined by `" | "`,
the form the Search API sends. In this package's development testing, this
field came back `NA` even on a live, otherwise fully entitled key, for documents
that do carry author keywords in 'Scopus' itself. This points to an entitlement
gap specific to this field. If your own keywords come back all `NA`, it is worth
raising with your Scopus/Elsevier account contact.

## References via Abstract Retrieval

The reference list is not available from Search under any view. It needs
Abstract Retrieval's `FULL` or `REF` view, an entitlement separate from
ordinary abstract access and from Search access. This is a per-document
endpoint, so retrieving references for *n* documents under `FULL` costs *n*
requests against Abstract Retrieval's own weekly quota, which is smaller than
Search's. Each row of the returned `references` data frame is one cited work.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ab <- scopus_abstract(
  "10.1038/nature14539",
  view = "FULL", include = c("references", "keywords")
)
ab$references[[1]][, c("title", "authors", "source", "year")]
```

`include = "keywords"` adds an `authkeywords` column, with the keywords joined
by `"; "` as the `authors` column joins names. The `references` list-column
holds one data frame per document, with the columns `position`, `id`, `doi`,
`title`, `authors`, `source`, `year` and `citedbycount`. Under `FULL`, a live
result writes each cited work's authors as surname and initials, such as
`"Doe, A."`, joined by `"; "`.

To show that shape offline, the chunk below relabels three bundled records into
those columns, as though they were works cited by a fourth document. They are
not the reference list of the document above, or of any other. These records
carry only each paper's first author, written as OpenAlex gives the name. `id`
holds a cited work's 'Scopus' identifier, absent from the bundled records, and
`citedbycount` is `NA` under `FULL`, so both are left `NA`.

```{r}
cited <- example_records[1:3, ]
refs <- tibble::tibble(
  position = as.character(seq_len(nrow(cited))),
  id = NA_character_,
  doi = cited$doi,
  title = cited$title,
  authors = cited$authors,
  source = cited$publication,
  year = cited$year,
  citedbycount = NA_integer_
)
refs[, c("title", "authors", "source", "year")]
```

`view = "FULL"` is the recommended default, since it returns the whole
bibliography in one request. `view = "REF"` serves it about 40 references at a
time. `scopus_abstract()` follows the view's `startref` parameter page by page
until the list is complete, so a document with *N* references costs
`ceiling(N / 40)` requests under `REF`. It warns when the number of references
it holds still does not match the document's own reported count.

The number of requests spent and the remaining Abstract Retrieval quota are
attached as attributes, since that smaller quota is easy to exhaust unnoticed.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
attr(ab, "n_requests")        # requests spent so far
attr(ab, "quota")$remaining   # Abstract Retrieval quota left
```

A key or subscription tier that does not cover the requested view raises a
`scopus_error_forbidden` condition that names the view. It also stops the whole
batch, because entitlement is a property of the account and the same error
would recur for every remaining identifier.

For more than a handful of identifiers, pass `cache_dir` so an interrupted or
quota-limited batch resumes without spending quota again on the identifiers it
has already retrieved.

```r
ab <- scopus_abstract(
  dois, view = "FULL", include = c("references", "keywords"),
  cache_dir = "abstract-cache"
)
```

## Index keywords

'Scopus' records a second kind of keyword. Authors choose their own keywords,
whereas 'Scopus' chooses the index keywords and standardises them to
vocabularies derived from thesauri Elsevier owns or licenses, with synonyms,
spellings and plurals brought together. `include = "index_terms"` adds them as
an `idxterms` column, joined by `"; "` as the author keywords are. Like the
author keywords, they come only with `view = "FULL"`, in the same request.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ab <- scopus_abstract(
  "10.1038/nature14539",
  view = "FULL", include = c("keywords", "index_terms")
)
ab$idxterms
```

Elsevier's guide lists index keywords in the `FULL` view as not available by
default, so whether they arrive depends on your key's entitlement. In this
package's development testing, they did arrive on the same key whose author
keywords came back empty. Where that happens, the index keywords may be the
only keyword signal a 'Scopus' harvest can give, but the two kinds are not
interchangeable. A standard vocabulary merges terms that authors phrase
differently, so the two give different co-occurrence networks from the same
documents, and a study should say which it used.

## A minimal, cross-tool corpus

`scopus_corpus()` combines a search result with this Abstract Retrieval step.
It returns a minimal shape close to what OpenAlex's `works` API already
returns: `id`, `scopus_id`, `title`, `year`, `keywords` (a list-column of
character vectors) and `references` (a list-column of data frames). A
bibliometrix data frame holds the references as semicolon-joined citation
strings instead. `scopus_corpus()` does not replace `as_bibliometrix()`, which
keeps its own field-mapping convention.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
recs <- scopus_fetch("DOI(10.1038/nature14539)", max_results = 1)
corpus <- scopus_corpus(recs, view = "FULL")
corpus$keywords[[1]]
nrow(corpus$references[[1]])
```

This costs one Abstract Retrieval request per record in `recs`, on top of
whatever retrieved `recs` in the first place. The `keywords` column, split from
the joined `authkeywords` string, holds a character vector per record, which is
the shape co-occurrence analysis needs. `keywords = "index"` fills it with the
index keywords instead, and `keywords = "both"` with the author keywords
followed by each index keyword not already among them. Either costs what the
default costs, and both need `view = "FULL"`. With `keywords = "both"`, the
match is on the exact text, so `"graphene"` from the author and `"Graphene"`
from the index both stay.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
corpus <- scopus_corpus(recs, view = "FULL", keywords = "both")
```

Counting every unordered pair of keywords within each document gives the
co-occurrence table the article opened on, and base R is enough for it. Author
keywords are one of the fields that cannot be included with the package, so the
corpus below replaces them with terms from each bundled record's own title. It
keeps a fixed vocabulary of terms and records those a title mentions. That is a
cruder signal than an author keyword list, but the counting is identical and it
runs over 138 published titles.

```{r}
vocabulary <- c("graphene", "supercapacitor", "electrode", "energy storage",
                "flexible", "electrochemical")
corpus <- tibble::tibble(
  id = example_records$doi,
  title = example_records$title,
  year = example_records$year,
  keywords = lapply(tolower(example_records$title), function(title) {
    vocabulary[vapply(vocabulary, grepl, logical(1), x = title, fixed = TRUE)]
  })
)
several <- corpus[lengths(corpus$keywords) > 1L, ]
head(data.frame(
  title = several$title,
  keywords = vapply(several$keywords, paste, character(1), collapse = "; ")
), 3)
```

```{r}
# Each unordered pair once per document, sorted in byte order, so the pairs and
# the order of tied counts do not depend on the locale.
pairs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(corpus$keywords, function(keywords) {
  if (length(keywords) < 2L) return(NULL)
  t(utils::combn(sort(keywords, method = "radix"), 2L))
}))
cooc <- as.data.frame(table(pairs[, 1], pairs[, 2]), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(cooc) <- c("keyword A", "keyword B", "documents")
cooc <- cooc[cooc$documents > 0L, ]
cooc <- cooc[order(-cooc$documents, cooc[["keyword A"]], cooc[["keyword B"]],
                   method = "radix"), ]
rownames(cooc) <- NULL
head(cooc, 5)
```

Each row is one pair of keywords and the number of documents carrying both,
which is the edge list a co-occurrence network is built from.

## Handing the corpus to theoryforge

theoryforge maps a literature from a corpus file in its own schema, and
`write_scopus_corpus()` writes one from a `scopus_corpus()` result. The file
needs a name for the corpus, since the result carries none.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write_scopus_corpus(corpus, "corpus.json", id = "graphene-supercapacitors")
```

theoryforge compares cited works as exact strings, so the writer gives each
one a single key across the corpus, its 'Scopus' identifier, as
`scopus:<id>`. 'Scopus' gives a cited work's DOI in some bibliographies only,
and in different cases. A key built from the DOI wherever there is one would
therefore split the work into several nodes and lose its co-citation edges. A
reference that carries only a DOI takes the identifier that another reference
pairs with the same DOI, and a DOI that nothing pairs with is keyed as
`doi:<doi>`, lower-cased. Keywords are lower-cased as well, so the
`"graphene"` and `"Graphene"` that `keywords = "both"` keeps apart become one.

The chunk below runs the writer on two bundled records, each made to cite the
same two others, the second with the DOIs in capitals. In the output, both
records cite the same two keys.

```{r}
docs <- example_records[!is.na(example_records$doi), ][1:4, ]
cites <- function(dois) tibble::tibble(id = NA_character_, doi = dois)
corpus <- tibble::tibble(
  id = docs$doi[1:2],
  scopus_id = NA_character_,
  title = docs$title[1:2],
  year = docs$year[1:2],
  keywords = list(c("Graphene", "supercapacitor"), "graphene"),
  references = list(cites(docs$doi[3:4]), cites(toupper(docs$doi[3:4])))
)
doc <- as_theoryforge_corpus(corpus, id = "graphene-supercapacitors")
doc$records[[1]]$references
doc$records[[2]]$references
```

The file also carries a `provenance` block recording the search expression,
when the search ran and the kind of keyword, with counts of the references
dropped and of the records without keywords. An entitlement that returns no
author keywords shows up in that last count, and it leaves theoryforge's
keyword themes empty whatever the writer does.
